claims.statement: An adaptation claim is interpretable only against a frozen behavior/configuration/evaluation baseline.
Target gains, retained capabilities, controls, resource budgets, and rejection criteria should precede training.
Upstream defects must be ruled out before attributing a failure to model weights.
Tokenizer, template, architecture, position/context mechanism, precision, and checkpoint are separate model-system surfaces.
Token fragmentation can change effective sequence length and multilingual/domain representation.
Architecture inspection identifies plausible intervention surfaces but cannot predict task improvement without experiments.
Prompt/context repair, SFT, PEFT, preference optimization, distillation, continued pretraining, and model replacement target different failure hypotheses.
Weight access, data quality, compute, reversibility, runtime, and control requirements constrain available interventions.
At least one plausible intervention should be rejected using predicted evidence or boundary constraints before experimentation expands.
A data recipe identifies sources, rights/permissions, example schema, inclusion/exclusion, quality, mixture, transformations, reviewers, versions, and limitations.
Synthetic instruction data can scale examples but may reproduce generator errors and biases.
Multilingual mixtures need explicit language/task balance and separate evaluation.
Deduplication can reduce memorization and evaluation contamination but thresholds and scope create tradeoffs.
Train, development, evaluation, retention, and control sets need explicit separation and identity.
Filtering and normalization choices alter the learned distribution and must be recorded as data decisions.
Instruction examples must map to target behavior clauses, errors, and segments rather than convenience prompts.
Chat template and loss masking determine which tokens contribute to SFT learning.
Negative, abstention, and boundary cases are needed when the contract requires non-answer behavior.
Preference data encodes a rubric, rater population, presentation order, and collection process rather than objective truth.
Position, verbosity, style, and self-preference biases can affect pairwise judgments.
Implicit production feedback is confounded by exposure, interface, incentives, and user selection unless designed as credible evidence.
Adaptation promotion requires target improvement plus retention, segment, and control regression evidence.
Language/domain gains can coexist with regressions outside the target mixture.
Safety/control cases and accountable owners must be preserved through adaptation rather than assumed from the base model.
A training run manifest needs base/tokenizer, data/splits, objective, optimizer/schedule, batch/sequence, precision, seeds, code, hardware class, checkpoints, and evaluators.
Mixed precision and sharding change memory/communication behavior and checkpoint procedures.
Training loss and resource completion do not establish target behavior improvement.
SFT optimizes likelihood on selected training tokens and therefore depends critically on data/template/masking choices.
Checkpoint selection should use held-out target, retention, segment, control, and resource evidence rather than minimum training loss.
Synthetic and multilingual training gains require independent held-out evaluation.
LoRA introduces trainable low-rank updates while freezing base weights, reducing trainable parameter/storage burden under studied conditions.
PEFT method support differs for layers, quantized bases, merging, hotswap, and runtime behavior.
An efficient adaptation must still pass the same target, retention, control, and inference compatibility evidence.
DPO optimizes a preference objective relative to a reference behavior without a separately trained explicit reward model in its original formulation.
Preference optimization can overfit biased or shortcut-bearing judgments, so independent behavior and retention evaluation is required.
Using the same model family to generate preferences, train, and judge can create coupled evidence that must be disclosed and independently checked.
Distillation transfers teacher behavior into a student under an explicit objective and data process; it is not generic compression magic.
Continued pretraining targets domain/task distribution through additional unsupervised language modeling and carries contamination/retention costs.
Advanced adaptation should be rejected when its hypothesis, data, resource, or evaluation burden is not distinct from a smaller intervention.
Deployable identity must bind base/checkpoint, tokenizer/template, adapter, config, schema, runtime, provenance/license, and integrity metadata.
Model cards document intended use, evaluation, and limitations but do not approve deployment.
Artifact format and checksums improve integrity/handling but do not prove provenance or behavioral compatibility.
Inference memory includes weights plus runtime state such as KV cache whose size depends on model, sequence, precision, and batch/concurrency.
Prefill and decode phases have different compute/memory behavior, and batching/caching/routing alter throughput and tail latency.
Task-level capacity models should record hardware/runtime/configuration and escalate kernel/platform work to adjacent specialists.
Quantization can reduce memory/compute cost but its quality and speed effects depend on method, model, calibration, hardware, and runtime.
Paged KV management, batching, caching, and speculative decoding can improve serving efficiency under bounded workloads.
Serving configuration must be selected on a measured behavior-resource frontier including protected segments and latency tails.
Adapted-model release needs target, retention, control, runtime, owner, observability, cohort, and rollback evidence.
Incident diagnosis must distinguish data, checkpoint/adapter, tokenizer/template, evaluator, runtime, and infrastructure changes.
A correction is incomplete until evidence, tests, controls, manifests, limitations, and monitoring are updated and replayed.
